questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a polyhedral convex set and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which pair of conditions guarantees that the set of global minimizers of $f$ on $D$ contains an extreme point of $D$?
options: $D$ is nonempty, and $f$ attains a global minimum on $D$.
$D$ has at least one extreme point, and $f$ attains a global maximum on $D$.
$D$ has at least one extreme point, and $f$ attains a global minimum on $D$.
$D$ has at least one extreme point, and one of them gives the smallest value of $f$ among the extreme points.

questions.question: Let $D$ be a polyhedral convex set with at least one extreme point, and let the affine function $f$ have global minimum value $m$ on $D$. The conclusion is written $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=m\}\cap\operatorname{Ext}(D)\neq\varnothing$. What does this statement say?
options: Some extreme point of $D$ is a global minimizer of $f$.
Every extreme point of $D$ is a global minimizer of $f$.
Every global minimizer of $f$ is an extreme point of $D$.
Exactly one extreme point of $D$ is a global minimizer of $f$.

questions.question: A linear program maximizes $Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over a polyhedral convex set $D$. It has at least one feasible corner point (an extreme point of $D$) and at least one optimal solution. Why can its optimal value be found by comparing finitely many numbers?
options: Every point of $D$ is a convex combination of its finitely many extreme points, so $Z$ is largest at one of them.
$D$ has finitely many extreme points, and at least one of them is optimal, so the optimal value is the largest $Z$ among them.
Every optimal solution is an extreme point of $D$, and $D$ has only finitely many extreme points to check.
An optimal solution exists only if $D$ is bounded, and a bounded polyhedral set has finitely many points to compare.

questions.question: The result on optima at extreme points takes $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ on a polyhedral convex set $D$ with at least one extreme point. What happens when $\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{0}$ is allowed?
options: $f$ has no minimum on an unbounded $D$, so the conclusion fails; $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is what guarantees an optimum.
The minimizers are the interior points of $D$, which are never extreme, so $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is essential.
$f$ is then not convex, so the result does not apply; $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ makes $f$ convex and concave.
$f$ is constant, so every point of $D$ is optimal and the conclusion holds; $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is not needed.

questions.question: To minimize $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ over a polyhedral convex set $D$ with an extreme point, on which $f$ attains a global minimum, picture the level sets $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=c\}$. Which description is correct?
options: Parallel hyperplanes along which $f$ falls as they move in direction $\boldsymbol{a}$; the last one still touching $D$ supports $D$.
Moving the parallel level hyperplanes in direction $-\boldsymbol{a}$ lowers $f$, and the last one meeting $D$ meets it in exactly one point.
Parallel hyperplanes; $f$ falls as they move in direction $-\boldsymbol{a}$, and at the last contact with $D$ the level set is a supporting hyperplane of $D$.
Moving the parallel level hyperplanes in direction $-\boldsymbol{a}$ lowers $f$ until they reach the point of $D$ nearest to the origin.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\geq4,\ -x_1+x_2\leq2,\ x_1-2x_2\leq1\}$, an unbounded polyhedral set with extreme points $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$. It is known that $f(\boldsymbol{x})=2x_1+3x_2-5$ attains a global minimum on $D$. What is that minimum value?

On $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq5,\ -x_1-x_2\leq-5,\ -x_1\leq0,\ -x_2\leq0\}$, whose extreme points are $(5,0)$ and $(0,5)$, take $f(\boldsymbol{x})=2x_1+2x_2+1$. Where does $f$ attain its global minimum and its global maximum on $D$?
options: Only $(5,0)$ and $(0,5)$ are minimizers and maximizers, since optima lie at extreme points.
The minimum $1$ is attained at $(0,0)$ and the maximum $21$ at $(5,5)$.
Since $\boldsymbol{a}=(2,2)\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, the minimizer and the maximizer are different extreme points.
$f=11$ on all of $D$, so every point of $D$ is both a minimizer and a maximizer.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\geq2\}$, a closed half-plane, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1+x_2$. Which statement about the global minimum of $f$ on $D$ is correct?
options: The minimum $2$ is attained on the whole line $x_1+x_2=2$, but $D$ has no extreme point.
The minimum $2$ is attained only at $(1,1)$, the extreme point of $D$ on the line $x_1+x_2=2$.
The minimum $2$ is attained at $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, the extreme points of $D$ on the axes.
$f$ has no minimum on $D$, because an affine function has no minimum on an unbounded set.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0,\ x_1+2x_2\geq4\}$, with extreme points $(4,0)$ and $(0,2)$, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1+3x_2$. Which statement about the global optima of $f$ on $D$ is correct?
options: The minimum $4$ is attained at $(4,0)$, and the maximum $6$ is attained at $(0,2)$.
The minimum $4$ is attained on the whole ray $\{(t,0)\colon t\geq4\}$, and there is no maximum.
The minimum $4$ is attained at $(4,0)$ only, and $f$ has no maximum on $D$.
$f$ is smallest at the origin, with value $0$, and is unbounded above on $D$.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq25\}$, a closed disc, which is compact and convex but not polyhedral, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=3x_1+4x_2$. Which statement about the global maximum of $f$ on $D$ is correct?
options: The maximum is $35$, attained at $(5,5)$, the corner of the box around $D$.
The maximum is $25$, attained only at $(3,4)$, an extreme point of $D$.
The maximum is $20$, attained at $(0,5)$, where the disc meets the $x_2$-axis.
No maximum is guaranteed, because the disc is not a polyhedral set.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ minimize $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i\ \forall i\}$. For $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{a}$ and to all $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ binding at $\boldsymbol{x}^*$, why is $\boldsymbol{x}^*+t\boldsymbol{d}$ a minimizer for small $|t|$?
options: $\boldsymbol{d}$ points in direction $-\boldsymbol{a}$, so $f$ only decreases and $\boldsymbol{x}^*+t\boldsymbol{d}$ stays at least as good.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is an interior point of $D$, so every point close to it lies in $D$ and has the same value of $f$.
$\boldsymbol{d}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{a}$, so the binding rows remain binding while $f$ keeps its minimal value.
$f$ keeps its value, binding rows stay binding, and nonbinding rows keep slack for small $|t|$.

questions.question: For a polyhedral convex set $D$, the result on optima at extreme points assumes that $D$ has an extreme point and that the optimum of the affine $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, exists. For a nonempty compact convex $D$ neither is assumed. Why?
options: $f$ is continuous, so it has optima on a compact set, and a nonempty compact convex set is the convex hull of its extreme points, so it has one.
Every nonempty compact convex set is polyhedral, so the polyhedral case applies, and boundedness then makes the optimum of $f$ exist.
An affine function attains its optima on every nonempty closed convex set, and a closed convex set always has an extreme point.
A bounded convex set has finitely many extreme points, so the optimum is simply the best of finitely many corner values.

questions.question: Let $D$ be a polyhedral convex set with at least one extreme point and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Suppose it is proved that a global minimum of every such $f$, if it exists, is attained at an extreme point. Why does the same hold for a global maximum?
options: An affine function is smallest at some extreme points and largest at all the others, so the maximizers are the remaining extreme points.
If $f$ has a global minimum on $D$, it also has a global maximum there, and the same argument puts both at extreme points.
A maximum $M$ of $f$ is a minimum $-M$ of $-f(\boldsymbol{x})=(-\boldsymbol{a})^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}-b$, which is again affine with a nonzero vector.
It holds only for bounded $D$, where the extreme value theorem gives the maximum; on an unbounded $D$ a maximum need not be extreme.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1-x_2\leq0,\ -x_1-x_2\leq0\}$, the region $x_2\geq|x_1|$, whose only extreme point is $(0,0)$, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1+x_2$. What is the set of global minimizers of $f$ on $D$?
options: Only the point $(0,0)$, the extreme point of $D$.
The ray $\{(-s,s)\colon s\geq0\}$, starting at the extreme point $(0,0)$.
The ray $\{(s,s)\colon s\geq0\}$ on the line $x_1=x_2$, starting at $(0,0)$.
Both boundary rays $\{(-s,s)\colon s\geq0\}$ and $\{(s,s)\colon s\geq0\}$.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq8$, $3x_1+x_2\leq9$, $x_1\geq0$, $x_2\geq0$. The feasible region is bounded. What is the optimal value?

Let $D$ be the closed triangle with corners $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}+b$ with an unknown $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ and $b$. All that is known is that $f$ attains its global minimum on $D$ at $(1,3)$. Which conclusion is correct?
options: $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$ are minimizers as well, and so is every point of the edge between them.
$(1,3)$ is the only minimizer, so here the minimum is attained at no extreme point of $D$.
$(0,4)$, the corner nearest to $(1,3)$, is a minimizer, but $(4,0)$ need not be one.
Every point of $D$ is a minimizer, since a minimizer that is not extreme makes $f$ constant on $D$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ minimize $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i\ \forall i\}$, with an extreme point $\boldsymbol{p}$; let $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ be orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{a}$ and the $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ binding at $\boldsymbol{x}^*$. Why must a new row bind at some $\boldsymbol{x}^*+t\boldsymbol{d}$?
options: Because $D$ is bounded, the line through $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ in direction $\boldsymbol{d}$ must leave $D$ on both sides.
Otherwise every row has $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=0$, so $\boldsymbol{p}\pm\boldsymbol{d}\in D$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is not extreme.
Otherwise $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ would decrease without bound along $\boldsymbol{x}^*+t\boldsymbol{d}$, contradicting that $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is a minimizer.
The minimizer $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is already an extreme point of $D$, so it cannot lie strictly inside a segment of $D$.

questions.question: A minimizer $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ of $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$, on $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i\ \forall i\}$, a set with an extreme point, is chosen so that $\boldsymbol{a}$ and the binding $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ contain as many linearly independent vectors as possible, say $r$. Why is $r=n$?
options: A minimizer with the most binding rows has at least $n$ of them, and $n$ rows binding at one point are always linearly independent.
If $r<n$, then $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ would be an interior point of $D$, and a minimizer of $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is never interior.
Since $D$ has an extreme point, every point of $D$ has $n$ linearly independent binding rows, the minimizer $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ included.
If $r<n$, moving along a suitable $\boldsymbol{d}$ gives a minimizer at which a new row binds, with a normal independent of the others: a larger count.

questions.question: Let $D=[0,1]\times[0,1]$ with the two points $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ removed, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_2$. Which statement about the minimum of $f$ on $D$ is correct?
options: $f$ has no minimum on $D$, because the two corners at which the minimum would be attained have been removed.
$\min f=0$ is attained at extreme points of $D$, because the points $(s,0)$ with $0<s<1$ become extreme once the corners are removed.
$\min f=0$ is attained only at the non-extreme points $(s,0)$, $0<s<1$; $D$ is not closed, hence not polyhedral.
$\min f=0$ is attained only at non-extreme points; this is possible because $D$ is not convex after removing two points.

questions.question: Let $D=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1,x_2,x_3\geq0,\ x_1+x_2+x_3\leq3,\ x_1\leq2\}$, a compact polyhedral set, and $f(\boldsymbol{x})=x_1+x_2+x_3$. What is the set of global maximizers of $f$ on $D$?
